transcript:
Header: 2026-10-05 16:00 PDT | Duration: 48m | Location: Zoom
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Lina Gomez (Redwood SE), Maya Rivera (Verdant CTO), Jon Park (Verdant ML Eng), Priya Singh (Verdant Security), Avery Cole (Verdant Product)

[00:00] Samir: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Samir from Redwood, this is Lina who's our SE. Quick check, audio/video good?
[00:10] Maya: Yep all good, thanks Samir.
[00:14] Lina: cool thank you. So today's plan quick 20 minute walkthrough of hosted API chat/text generation basics, show streaming, talk params, retries, and then leave time for questions and next steps.
[00:24] Jon: Sounds good, mostly interested in streaming latency and how we tune model randomness for our summarization use case.
[00:32] Priya: And security questions around data retention, KMS, and SOC2.
[00:37] Samir: Great, we'll cover those. I'll start high level then Lina will demo.

[02:05] Samir: Quick context question - what's your current stack for inference? Are you running anything in-house or using an API?
[02:12] Maya: We're using a mix - some internal models on k8s and we use OpenAI API for prod features; cost is rising and latency is variable.
[02:21] Jon: We also batch some requests which helps cost but hurts latency; want something predictable.
[02:26] Samir: Got it. Typical. Hosted API is often the fastest path. We provide streaming token-by-token, per-route dashboards, and cost controls. Lina will demo the streaming endpoint and show how you can set params like temperature, max_tokens, top_p.

[04:40] Lina: Ok sharing screen - here's a simple curl example we use in docs. (screen shows code) curl -X POST https://api.redwood.ai/v1/chat -H "Authorization: Bearer $REDWOOD_KEY" -d '{"model":"redwood-1.5-chat","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Summarize our Q3 roadmap"}],"stream":true,"temperature":0.2,"max_tokens":150}'
[04:58] Lina: When stream:true we open an SSE/HTTP stream and you'll get chunks back incrementally. This reduces first-byte latency and UX snappiness for chat UIs.
[05:12] Jon: Is stream over HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2? We have multiplexing concerns.
[05:17] Lina: We support both, SSE over HTTP/1.1 is common; we also have a websocket SDK for real-time apps. If you need massive multiplexing, we recommend HTTP/2 or websocket.

[07:05] Lina: Demo time - I'll run a few prompts. Note there may be minor transcription weirdness with the live demo.
[07:12] Speaker 2: (inaudible)
[07:18] Lina: First - deterministic summaries: set temperature=0 or 0.1 and top_p=1, set max_tokens to control length. For more creative outputs, bump temperature to 0.7.
[07:30] Samir: Also top_k isn't necessary for most models but we expose it if you have custom sampling needs.

[09:02] Maya: For our summarization we need consistent tone and short outputs - what's best practice?
[09:07] Lina: Temperature 0-0.2, top_p 0.8-1, max_tokens 80-150 depending. We also recommend system prompts with explicit style rules, and use stop sequences to enforce truncation.

[11:40] Jon: How does streaming affect cost? We pay per token emitted right?
[11:45] Samir: Correct you pay per input and output tokens. Streaming doesn't change pricing per-token, but it can reduce perceived latency and allow optimistic UI rendering; it may increase tokens if you do incremental prompts or partial retries, so watch for that.

[13:21] Lina: About retries - we have idempotency keys you can pass with requests to avoid duplicate consumption if a retry succeeds after a network flake. Also clients should implement exponential backoff (we recommend 500ms base, 2x factor, jitter, max attempts 4).
[13:45] Lina: Example header: "Idempotency-Key: <uuid>" and we also return a request id in the response for correlation.

[15:00] Jon: Does Redwood auto-retry on some 5xx?
[15:05] Lina: We have some server-side transient retries, but we also recommend client-side controlled retries for network issues. For streaming specifically, a disconnect means you can re-open the stream and resume if you use KV cache / context rehydration on your side; we provide session tokens to help reconstruct state. There's not a perfect resume for in-flight token stream yet, so usually you either re-request last N messages or use partial caching.

[17:40] Priya: On security - our compliance team needs to know about data retention and key management. Where is data stored and is customer data encrypted at rest?

[17:50] Samir: Hosted API is SOC2 compliant (we'll send cert). Data at rest is encrypted, KMS options available for enterprise customers; we also support bring-your-own-key (BYOK) for higher tiers. We keep audit logs per request and you can set data retention policy.
[18:10] Priya: Any concerns about PII passing through? We need guaranteed deletion requests and audit trails.
[18:17] Lina: Yes, we have delete endpoints and retention settings; enterprise plan gives you longer retention and better exportable audit logs. We'll attach the security docs post-call.

[20:55] Lina: Back to params - we can also throttle or limit per-route. The Console allows per-route quotas and you can pin models to routes. In the Console you'll see token-level cost, per-request latency histograms, and traces to see where time's spent (network, model compute, queuing).

[22:03] Maya: Do you have burst capacity protection? We sometimes have traffic spikes.
[22:10] Samir: For hosted customers we provide burst windows and soft quotas; for strict capacity and SLA you can choose Dedicated. Hosted has elastic capacity but SLA tiers vary by commitment level.

[24:40] Jon: Curious about batching - you mentioned Optimize recommendations. How does that work?
[24:46] Lina: Optimize analyzes your usage patterns and recommends batching or cache settings. For very short queries batching can reduce unit cost but raises latency; Optimize will suggest per-route batch sizing and when to enable prefix/KV caching for repeated prefixes such as prompts for summarization.

[26:10] Jon: For our use case we have lots of short summarize calls, would kv cache help?
[26:16] Lina: Yes if prompts share a common prefix or system prompt, KV cache can save repeated compute. Quantization suggestions may also help on Dedicated for throughput/cost tradeoffs.

[28:30] Maya: Any limitations on max request size or context window?
[28:35] Lina: Current hosted models support up to 32k tokens for some variants; default is 8k for the mid-tier models. We'll include model catalog with supported context lengths.

[30:12] Priya: Encryption in transit? TLS only?
[30:15] Samir: TLS 1.2+ by default; mTLS options for Dedicated/Private. SSO via SAML/OIDC for Console access.

[31:40] Lina: Demo - I'll show a Python SDK snippet for streaming. (shows code)
[31:45] Lina: from redwood import RedwoodClient
client = RedwoodClient(api_key="$REDWOOD_KEY")
for chunk in client.chat.stream(model="redwood-1.5-chat", messages=msgs, temperature=0.2):
    print(chunk.text, end='')

[33:00] Jon: Nice. If a chunk is dropped mid-stream can we re-request and dedupe?
[33:06] Lina: Use idempotency keys and request ids; for UX we recommend keeping the last few messages client-side and re-syncing if needed. Also we expose request/response ids in Console traces for debugging.

[35:20] Maya: What's the expected latency for first token?
[35:24] Lina: Depends on model size and sequence length; typical p95 first-byte for our mid models is 120-300ms in us-west region under nominal load. We'll share benchmark dashboards.

[37:05] Jon: For stress tests, do you provide benchmarking harness or a load test plan?
[37:11] Samir: Yes we have a benchmark harness and we can run a joint test during POC to validate latency and cost. Often we do a pilot with a traffic replay.

[39:40] Priya: On legal/procurement side, do you have standard DPA and terms?
[39:45] Samir: Yes we include DPA and standard enterprise addenda for data residency and compliance. We'll route those through your procurement and legal.

[41:30] Avery: Product question - can we do function/tool calling or structure outputs?
[41:36] Lina: Yes we support structured output and function calling primitives; you can declare function schemas and get JSON outputs. Works with both streaming and non-streaming modes.

[43:10] Samir: Ok let's recap - next steps: we'll send pricing + token cost examples, Lina will share demo notebook and SDK snippets, security docs and SOC2, and we'll propose POC times. Anything else?
[43:28] Maya: Please include estimated monthly cost for 500k and 2M tokens for a couple model options.
[43:34] Samir: noted.

[45:00] Priya: I'll email over a compliance checklist.
[45:04] Samir: Great, thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the items listed.
[45:12] Speaker 1: thanks
[45:15] Speaker 3: bye

[47:50] (call ends)
